The Harmonized Interior

The World Beyond the Frontier

Not all lands are broken.

Beyond the frontier lie the Harmonized Interior: regions where the Great Work has already been carried forward as far as it can be without the whole world being reclaimed. These lands are not perfect, and they are not identical, but they are stable. Their hexes are named, organized, inhabited, aligned, and held in relationship with one another. Their sparks have largely been reclaimed, purified, and put to use. Their people live within systems that function well enough that many no longer remember how miraculous that is.

This does not mean these lands are utopias.

The Harmonized Interior still contains rivalry, inequality, bureaucracy, corruption, grief, local prejudice, political struggle, and deep philosophical disagreement. The difference is that these tensions are held within structures strong enough to prevent total collapse. The darkness is managed rather than ascendant. Civilization persists because enough people continue the work of maintaining it.

In these lands, the Great Work is not just a miracle of the past. It is an ongoing civic, spiritual, logistical, and moral commitment.

The frontier matters because the world is still incomplete.

There are still dark hexes. Still broken territories. Still unreclaimed sparks. Still ruined systems, wounded places, half-stabilized regions, old scars, old vaults, old sins, and old hungers. The civilized lands endure, but they do not endure alone. The unfinished world presses on them. What remains wild, wounded, or corrupted affects everything.

That is why people still go outward.

Some go because they are called. Some because they are assigned. Some because they are idealists, opportunists, refugees, debtors, seekers, penitents, believers, scholars, surveyors, or fools. Some go to help. Some go to prove themselves. Some go because civilized life has become too narrow for the shape of their soul.

Your character comes from somewhere.

They may be from an orderly core region, a reclaimed near-edge province, a mobile trade culture, a scholastic enclave, a subterranean mutual-aid network, or some other place where people have already learned how to keep the world from slipping entirely apart.

What matters is this:

The frontier is not where civilization begins.
It is where civilization is tested.

Journal: GM Canon Note — The Harmonized Interior

Canon Frame

Use the following as the baseline for Bad Eden homeland backstories.

The “civilized world” consists of regions where the Great Work has already been substantially completed at the local scale. In these lands:

  • Hexes are claimed, named, and integrated into wider systems.
  • Most sparks have been reclaimed and purified.
  • Darkness exists, but is manageable rather than existential.
  • Infrastructure exists in practical and mystical forms: roads, archives, market routes, signal systems, ley management, weather stabilization, fortified settlements, rigs, shrines, and civic institutions.
  • Multiple non-Qliphothic alignments are acceptable.
  • Civilization is maintained through coalition, ritual, labor, and vigilance rather than monoculture.

These lands are not perfect. They are post-crisis societies that survived metaphysical catastrophe and then institutionalized the cure. Their citizens may disagree bitterly about politics, philosophy, faith, economics, and governance, but they broadly accept that the darkness must not be allowed to rule.

This means characters can come from real places with real institutions, real habits, and real assumptions before arriving at the frontier.

The frontier is where:

  • harmonization is incomplete
  • systems remain unstable
  • dark pressure remains high
  • reclamation is still active and dangerous
  • ethics must be practiced under stress rather than merely preached in safety

The civilized lands are best understood as cooperation under metaphysical pressure.

Journal: The Avuncular Marches

The Avuncular Marches

The Avuncular Marches are orderly, cultivated, and deeply maintained lands where care has been made into a public discipline.

These are regions of civic gardens, repaired canals, measured growth, stable settlements, and institutions built not merely to endure, but to reassure. Public works are maintained with near-religious seriousness. Archives are current. Roads are clear. Children are taught spark ethics alongside practical literacy. Local officials are expected to know the names of the people under their care, and failure to maintain systems is treated not simply as negligence, but as moral breach.

The people of the Marches often believe civilization is something tender that must be protected through diligence, structure, and memory. They remember very well that softness only exists because someone fought for the right to have it.

Outsiders sometimes regard the Marches as smothering, paternal, or over-managed. Those from the Marches often reply that unmanaged systems are how worlds die.

Common Values

  • stewardship
  • continuity
  • maintenance
  • public duty
  • humane structure

Common Visuals

  • canalworks humming with quiet resonance control
  • old fortifications converted into schools, clinics, and councils
  • boundary shrines and wardstones built into everyday infrastructure
  • green public spaces laid deliberately over reclaimed scars
  • official buildings that feel warm rather than grand

Why People Leave

  • assigned to frontier service by civic or spiritual authorities
  • a sincere desire to extend care into unstable lands
  • frustration with managed life and narrow expectations
  • family duty, debt, or inherited obligation
  • the need to prove that their values survive outside protected systems

What Marchers Often Assume About the Frontier

  • that frontier life is less organized than it needs to be
  • that suffering is often prolonged by avoidable neglect
  • that many local disasters would be smaller with better maintenance

What the Frontier Often Gets Wrong About Marchers

  • that they are soft
  • that they are naive
  • that kindness means weakness

Character Prompts

You may be:

  • a junior official trained in systems maintenance
  • a community-minded healer or harmonizer
  • someone fleeing benevolent suffocation
  • an idealist who actually believes institutions can be good
  • a careful soul learning how to function where the rails end

Journal: The Attackountant Coalition States

The Attackountant Coalition States

The coalition states governed or influenced by the Attackountants are lands where accountability has been elevated into both civic doctrine and cultural instinct.

These regions are efficient without necessarily being joyless, disciplined without necessarily being cruel, and deeply suspicious of anything that cannot be measured, audited, or traced to consequence. Resource flows are tracked. Public expenditure is visible. Transit is logged. Losses are investigated. Corruption is treated not merely as theft, but as sabotage against collective survival.

The coalition worldview is simple in principle: if the world is hard, then systems must be clear. If survival is collective, then obligations must be legible. If people are entrusted with power, then they must be answerable for what they do with it.

This produces impressive infrastructure, stable supply chains, high institutional competence, and a culture that tends to reward precision. It also produces burnout, perfectionism, political severity, and a habit of turning human complexity into administrative language.

Still, when the lights stay on, the grain arrives, the weather stations report, the market routes hold, and the numbers reconcile, many citizens view the bargain as worth it.

Common Values

  • accountability
  • clarity
  • disciplined labor
  • anti-corruption ethics
  • measurable stewardship

Common Visuals

  • public ledgers posted in civic squares
  • signal towers, depots, and supply hubs run with visible precision
  • fortified warehouses and rig yards kept in immaculate order
  • administrative offices that feel as important as temples
  • charts, route maps, and audit marks built into daily life

Why People Leave

  • official deployment to unstable regions
  • faith in structure and a desire to fix failing systems
  • personal disgrace or institutional conflict
  • Stress with being measured at every turn
  • desire to test theory against the actual chaos of the world

What Coalition Folk Often Assume About the Frontier

  • that waste is everywhere
  • that local failure usually has a procedural cause
  • that good intentions without systems are a death sentence

What the Frontier Often Gets Wrong About Coalition Folk

  • that they care only about numbers
  • that order means cruelty
  • that procedure and compassion cannot coexist

Character Prompts

You may be:

  • a field auditor or logistics specialist
  • a reformer who hates corruption more than they hate conflict
  • an efficient operator learning mercy
  • someone cast out by an institution they once served
  • a person trying to prove that rigor can save lives without devouring them

Journal: The Free Peoples of Underground Montana

The Free Peoples of Underground Montana

The Free Peoples of Underground Montana are not one nation so much as a living network of tunnel communities, vault settlements, hidden markets, defended routes, old shelters, adapted bunkers, and proud local cultures bound together by memory and mutual reliance.

These are peoples who survived because they helped one another when nobody else was coming.

Their cultures tend to prize practical solidarity over polished theory, competence over status, and trust earned through action over trust granted by office. Their institutions are often local, layered, improvised, and fiercely defended. They are not necessarily anti-organization, but they are deeply suspicious of distant authority that has not bled for them.

Their settlements often carry the marks of adaptation: old infrastructure repurposed into homes, communal chambers built into once-military spaces, generators and shrines side by side, civic life emerging from salvage and stubbornness. Their stories emphasize survival, kinship, memory, and the refusal to let each other disappear.

They may seem rough to outsiders. To themselves, they are simply real.

Common Values

  • mutual aid
  • local autonomy
  • earned trust
  • stubborn survival
  • communal defense

Common Visuals

  • tunnel settlements lit by reclaimed systems and careful improvisation
  • old vault architecture adapted into homes, commons, workshops, and shrines
  • patchworked infrastructure that works because people care enough to keep it working
  • communal kitchens, market halls, and assembly spaces built into hard stone
  • visible signs of repair, reuse, and multigenerational endurance

Why People Leave

  • called to serve beyond their home routes
  • sent as scouts, traders, negotiators, or defenders
  • a belief that survival should not be hoarded
  • conflict with local custom or kin authority
  • hunger for open sky, wider maps, or a cause larger than the home network

What Underground Folk Often Assume About the Frontier

  • that people survive there by trust or die by pride
  • that “civilized” plans often break on first contact with reality
  • that nobody gets through alone for long

What the Frontier Often Gets Wrong About Underground Folk

  • that they are backward
  • that they are provincial
  • that informal systems are weaker than formal ones

Character Prompts

You may be:

  • a convoy child or tunnel scout
  • a community defender
  • a salvage scholar or rig mechanic
  • a fiercely loyal soul with no patience for empty status
  • someone learning how to trust institutions without abandoning your instincts

Journal: The Sephirotic Enclaves

The Sephirotic Enclaves

The Sephirotic enclaves are places where metaphysical literacy is taken as seriously as engineering, law, or medicine.

These are observatories, correspondence halls, alignment schools, ritual gardens, archive-temples, resonance labs, and disciplined communities where the structure of meaning is studied as a practical necessity. Their citizens are often taught from an early age that symbols matter, alignment matters, naming matters, memory matters, and carelessness in spiritual or conceptual systems can become material disaster.

The enclaves are not uniform in doctrine, but they broadly agree that civilization survives when the world is interpreted responsibly. This makes them home to scholars, ritualists, harmonizers, archivists, signal readers, and deeply serious people trying to keep understanding from becoming either empty abstraction or dangerous arrogance.

To outsiders, these places may feel overthought, ceremonial, or impossibly precise. To the enclaves, this is simply what it looks like to take reality seriously.

These are places of beauty, discipline, and burden.

Common Values

  • balance
  • interpretation
  • ethical knowledge
  • disciplined practice
  • responsible power

Common Visuals

  • resonance gardens laid out according to philosophical correspondences
  • towers and chambers built for study, signal-reading, and ritual calibration
  • annotated public spaces filled with symbols that actually mean something
  • archives protected like sacred organs
  • communities where ceremony and technical procedure overlap seamlessly

Why People Leave

  • sent to study unstable regions directly
  • pursuing insight that cannot be found in safe conditions
  • burdened by prophecy, omen, correspondence, or calling
  • exiled by doctrinal conflict or interpretive dissent
  • need to test theory against lived catastrophe

What Enclave Folk Often Assume About the Frontier

  • that many crises are worsened by ignorance of deeper patterns
  • that language, ritual, and symbol are treated too casually
  • that people often stumble into corruption before they understand what they are touching

What the Frontier Often Gets Wrong About Enclave Folk

  • that they are detached from reality
  • that they care more about ideas than people
  • that ritual precision is vanity rather than safety

Character Prompts

You may be:

  • an apprentice harmonizer or ritual engineer
  • a scholar fleeing a doctrinal cage
  • a mystic burdened with too much understanding
  • an archivist who knows memory can save worlds
  • someone who believes wisdom means going where it hurts

Journal: The Market Roads and Corridor Republics

The Market Roads and Corridor Republics

The Market Roads and Corridor Republics are regions held together less by shared ancestry or single doctrine than by exchange, movement, negotiated peace, and mutual need.

These are caravan states, trade cities, route compacts, rig ports, relay stations, transit republics, and crossroads territories where many peoples meet because they must. Goods move through them. News moves through them. Specialists, pilgrims, enforcers, mercenaries, diplomats, outcasts, and saints all pass through them. So do rumors, diseases, relics, philosophies, and trouble.

Life in these places tends to make people practical about difference. You may dislike your neighbors. You may distrust them. You may argue endlessly. But if the road closes, everyone suffers. If the depots fail, everyone hungers. If the route wards break, everyone pays.

This creates cultures that are often cosmopolitan, fast-talking, suspicious, adaptive, and unusually good at surviving through negotiation. Their weakness is that everything can begin to feel transactional. Their strength is that they have learned how to make coexistence profitable enough to endure.

Common Values

  • exchange
  • flexibility
  • negotiation
  • mobility
  • pluralism under pressure

Common Visuals

  • fortified roads, rest stations, relay towers, and market depots
  • public squares full of mixed languages, fashions, and customs
  • rigs and caravans treated as both commerce and civic lifeline
  • civic law built around passage, contract, and shared risk
  • shrines and tradehouses standing side by side

Why People Leave

  • trade missions or escort work
  • diplomatic or mercantile ambition
  • debt, exile, or reputation trouble
  • hunger for a place where values matter more than transaction
  • belief that stable routes require stable frontiers

What Corridor Folk Often Assume About the Frontier

  • that isolation creates avoidable extremity
  • that people there underestimate the value of interdependence
  • that roads are moral instruments, not just physical ones

What the Frontier Often Gets Wrong About Corridor Folk

  • that they are rootless
  • that they only care about profit
  • that compromise means lack of conviction

Character Prompts

You may be:

  • caravan-born
  • a merchant negotiator or route scout
  • a fixer, interpreter, or convoy guard
  • someone raised among constant human difference
  • a person trying to prove that connection is stronger than fear

Journal: The Reclaimed Edge Provinces

The Reclaimed Edge Provinces

The Reclaimed Edge Provinces are stable lands, but only recently.

These are places where the darkness was pushed back within living memory. Their roads are new over old scars. Their shrines stand beside ruins. Their councils are often young, their rituals practical, and their civic pride sharp with the memory of how much it cost to get here.

People from these provinces are often intensely vigilant. They know civilization is not a natural condition. They know what it looks like when systems fail, when old certainties die, when the wrong thing moves in, when whole districts go quiet, when neighbors become Shaken, cruel, or strange. They know what reclamation requires.

As a result, these provinces often produce deeply capable people who can seem severe, proud, suspicious, or hard to impress. But they also produce some of the fiercest believers in hope, because they have watched impossible recovery happen with their own eyes.

They are civilized lands with smoke still in the walls.

Common Values

  • vigilance
  • earned hope
  • resilience
  • practical solidarity
  • memory of cost

Common Visuals

  • new settlements built against the bones of damaged predecessors
  • repaired walls, fresh wards, and visible memorials
  • reclaimed civic centers still carrying the marks of triage
  • shrines to the lost maintained alongside infrastructure for the living
  • people who can point to exactly where things went wrong, and where they were won back

Why People Leave

  • frontier service feels like a continuation of home’s unfinished work
  • hunger to prevent other places from suffering what theirs did
  • restlessness born from growing up amid reconstruction
  • difficulty living among people who want to move on faster than they do
  • desire to test hard-earned values somewhere they matter

What Edge Folk Often Assume About the Frontier

  • that danger is always closer than people think
  • that complacency kills
  • that hope without readiness is sentimentality

What the Frontier Often Gets Wrong About Edge Folk

  • that they are joyless
  • that suspicion means cruelty
  • that severity means lack of imagination

Character Prompts

You may be:

  • the child of reclaimers, wardens, or local defenders
  • someone who grew up rebuilding what others abandoned
  • a survivor who cannot stop scanning for cracks
  • a believer in hope because you have seen it bleed and still survive
  • a person carrying both pride and unresolved grief

Journal: Homeland Backstory Prompts

Quick Backstory Questions

Use these to develop your character’s origins before arriving at the frontier.

1. What kind of homeland shaped you?

Were you raised in order, improvisation, scholarship, exchange, vigilance, or communal survival?

2. What did your people believe civilization was for?

Safety? Freedom? Accountability? Balance? Connection? Memory? Shared labor?

3. What part of your homeland do you still defend instinctively?

Its values? Its habits? Its people? Its systems? Its dignity?

4. What part of it are you resisting or trying to escape?

Its expectations? Its blind spots? Its hierarchy? Its complacency? Its demands?

5. Why did you come to the frontier?

Duty, faith, ambition, exile, grief, curiosity, debt, service, hope, hunger, or something stranger?

6. What does the frontier misunderstand about people like you?

What assumption do others make when they hear where you are from?

7. What are you afraid might be true?

That your homeland was wrong?
That it was right?
That its values only work in safe places?
That you are more like it than you wanted to be?

Journal: Short Player Summary

Choosing a Homeland

Pick the homeland that feels most like the world that made you.

You are not choosing a perfect nation or a permanent ideology. You are choosing the kind of society that raised you before you came to a place where everything is harder, stranger, and less settled.

Your character may love their homeland, resent it, miss it, reject it, defend it, or carry it like an old wound.

What matters is that they came from somewhere real.

The frontier is where the world is unfinished.

You are here because, one way or another, so are you.
